title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
description: Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has
body: Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report."Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick. While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

schema.headline: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling

title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
description: French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.Arnould, w
body: French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play. She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic. Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us". Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation. He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020. Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules

title: Guinea orders mass clean-up in Conakry months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
description: Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.Prime
body: Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December  to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs."The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said."Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in Baretodé, outside the capital.The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

schema.headline: Guinea orders mass clean-up in Conakry months after deadly rubbish dump collapse

title: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza
description: A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.Local sour
body: A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month."No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

schema.headline: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza

title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News InvestigationsA German
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News InvestigationsA German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police. Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled) At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.Image caption, One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cansThe case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show."Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boatsBoth men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.Image caption, Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German policeMeanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.Image caption, We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rulesWhen we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.Image caption, Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near DortmundIn Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
description: Figure caption, Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's musicByMusic correspondentUpdated 5 hours agoSimon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewa
body: Figure caption, Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's musicByMusic correspondentUpdated 5 hours agoSimon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music."His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart"."Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."Figure caption, Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order,  recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You. Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songsThe son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and new wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980sDuran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs. Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station. The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid."We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy. "We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.Image source, PAImage caption, Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse MacabreAfter a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again. In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion. When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor: Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMTSounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT

schema.headline: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65

title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
description: France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027,  unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.Wit
body: France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027,  unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge."The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.In the last two weeks, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, a majority of Communist parliamentary deputies and one-time Socialist presidential hopeful Benoît Hamon have all thrown in their lot with the leader of France Unbowed (LFI).Another prominent figure of the left – François Ruffin – has also withdrawn from the race, bowing to the unbowed Mélenchon's now almost total command of the field.So with the soft-left emasculated,  the main hope for an alternative to Le Pen and Mélenchon has to be focused on the right.  But here the prospects – which until recently seemed bright – are now clouded with gloom."A Mélenchon–Le Pen duel in round two is not yet inevitable," says Guillaume Tabard, political analyst at the conservative Le Figaro newspaper.  "But it is looking increasingly probable."In recent weeks the poll ratings of the main centre-right hopeful Edouard Philippe – a former prime minister under President Macron – have fallen sharply, and he is now consistently placed behind Mélenchon in the first round of the vote.  Marine Le Pen is way ahead of both.Other candidates for command of this centre-right "space" are circling.  They include another former Macron prime minister, Gabriel Attal;  the leader of the right-wing Republicans (and former Macron interior minister), Bruno Retailleau;  and now – a surprise new challenger – the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard.Lisnard, who stands on a liberal economic platform of less state and lower taxes, has emerged from nowhere to become the man of the hour. Membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie (New Energy) has shot up to more than 100,000, and he is being taken seriously as a possible Philippe replacement.But this very multiplicity of names – not to mention others like judoka Teddy Riner, journalist Natacha Polony and former prime minister Dominique de Villepin – betrays the essential weakness of the centre-right challenge.According to veteran commentator Nicolas Baverez, "If you want to win an election, it's quite simple: you need a strategy, a programme, and activists.  Right now in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon we have none of that: there is a total vacuum."The most glaring absence is digital. Mélenchon especially, but Le Pen too, are running extremely effective social media campaigns.  In the middle… nothing."Guillaume Tabard agrees that the lack of a shared platform is proving a serious handicap."In recent weeks we have seen Marine Le Pen issue her manifesto proposals for reforming pensions.  We have seen Jean-Luc Mélenchon publish his programme in a best-selling book," he says."What do we have in between? Arguments about names and polling figures and whether or not there should be a primary.  It's not, to put it mildly, an encouraging start."For Fressoz, "There is no-one in the centre who is taking up the fight. When Le Pen makes her proposals about pensions, there is no-one saying, 'Hang on, that doesn't add up!'.  Macron – who did after all take her on and beat her – is said to be furious."Any mention of Macron, though, is most unwelcome for the camp that nominally is his heir. Philippe, Attal and Retailleau all served under a president who Baverez now calls "as toxic as Trump", so deep is his unpopularity in the country. Lisnard, by contrast, makes much of his refusal to serve under Macron – but he faces another handicap.According to Fressoz, "Lisnard has shot up in the polls because he is on the right of the right, and there is always an appetite for a figure who is not Le Pen, but who speaks her kind of language on immigration."But Lisnard is an economic liberal, and in France that is a minority taste. He'll have his moment but then he will deflate."With five months to go to until the election, all is not lost for the mainstream. Optimists in its ranks say that come the new year, opinion polls will start settling behind one or other centre-right candidate, and the others will feel obliged to step aside.Talk of a centre-right primary – as occurred ahead of the 2017 election – is beginning to ebb.  The two strongest candidates, Philippe and Lisnard, are opposed. Lisnard says he supports one but his conditions are designed to be unacceptable to the rest. Retailleau and Attal are in favour – but that, says Tabard, is "mainly as a way to keep their hopes alive."In theory then it is possible a name will emerge in January or February, and start pulling behind him (or less likely, her) the mass of voters who do not want a disruptive radical as France's next head of state.Possible, but hardly a good bet.For Fressoz of Le Monde, "After years of Macron's 'neither left nor right', the left and right are once again shaping French politics. But now it is the extremes who are in control."Le Pen and Mélenchon have both already run three times for the presidency. Their visions were defined long ago, their strategies laid, their activists trained.  Polarisation is their friend,  so is the social tension of recent weeks, and both are undisputed masters in their own camps.The 2027 dénouement has been in their sights for years. That is their massive advantage.

schema.headline: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate

title: Wang Fuk Court: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
description: It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.At around
body: It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user -  was trapped inside their home."I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said. Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second -  an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report."It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet."He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin"."I would have held onto my husband and died with him."He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park."All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells. Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her."My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it. Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father. Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family."He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art. She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight. Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the tragedy the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years."Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house. The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said."Should I say that we are fortunate?"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out. The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.

schema.headline: Wang Fuk Court: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168

title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
description: An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.Eyewitnesses share
body: An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery. On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges. It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

schema.headline: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion

title: Med Emre: Diesel tanker carrying tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
description: An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.The Med E
body: An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service."There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

schema.headline: Med Emre: Diesel tanker carrying tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one

title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
description: The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.The treaties were published on Thur
body: The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released. Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements.""It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning. However, the UK will not be given voting rights.Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny. Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

schema.headline: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause

title: Indonesia: 13 dead in mine disaster that highlights illegal hunt for gold
description: It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground
body: It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims."We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday."The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures."[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector."It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments"."As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects. Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear"."Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it."This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman."We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched."Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

schema.headline: Indonesia: 13 dead in mine disaster that highlights illegal hunt for gold

title: More than 1,000 flights cancelled or delayed in US as weather disrupts Thanksgiving travel
description: Figure caption, Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North AmericaByAna FaguyJames FitzGerald and Sareen HabeshianUpdated 20 minutes ag
body: Figure caption, Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North AmericaByAna FaguyJames FitzGerald and Sareen HabeshianUpdated 20 minutes agoNearly 400 flights in the US have been cancelled so far on Thursday as bad weather coincides with busy travel on the Thanksgiving holiday.Another 1,200 flights into, out of, or within the US have been delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.On Wednesday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) briefly grounded all flights heading for Miami International Airport after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway. No injuries were reported, and the FAA is investigating.More than 80 million Americans were expected to be traveling this week at the same time the National Weather Service (NWS) has forecast storms along the western and eastern coasts of the US that could bring heavy rain and flooding.Figure caption, FedEx aircraft sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway The FAA previously warned that delays across the country would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast. On Wednesday, FlightAware reported more than 6,800 delays and more than 160 cancellations.The NWS forecast a strong storm will deluge the eastern US coast on Thursday, bringing high winds, heavy rainfall and major coastal flooding. Ahead of expected severe weather in New Jersey, the state's governor, Mikie Sherrill, declared a state of emergency. Several coastal areas that experienced flooding earlier this autumn could be vulnerable again on Thursday.In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.Image source, Getty ImagesMany are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.In Miami, some travel delays persist after the FedEx plane incident prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period on Wednesday evening.Figure caption, High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communitiesA statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor."They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over Thanksgiving, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

schema.headline: More than 1,000 flights cancelled or delayed in US as weather disrupts Thanksgiving travel

title: Muhoozi Kainerugaba: Ugandan president's son angers DR Congo with social media posts
description: The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainer
body: The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns. The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.The Ugandan government has yet to respond.The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours. Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province. They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo. "These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday. "The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future". The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

schema.headline: Muhoozi Kainerugaba: Ugandan president's son angers DR Congo with social media posts

title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
description: US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approva
body: US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind. The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth". "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said. Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them."That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."

schema.headline: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
